text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Wednesday.

GERMANY - German debt remained at higher levels in late trading on Wednesday with dealers forecasting range-trade for the next sessions as the market eyes year-end holiday celebrations and feels ever less inclined to trade. The March Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 100.06, up 0.23 from Tuesday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilts fought back to end Wednesday unchanged after plummeting in morning trade following the release of very strong employment and retail sales data. The March long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 108-23/32 up 01/32 from Tuesday's settlement price.

FRANCE - March bond futures settled slightly higher after a quiet session, stuck in 10-tick range, volume low. March PIBOR got early boost from call money cut but weaker franc weighed. The March notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 128.46 up 0.12 from Tuesday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian bond futures held to firmer levels in late afternoon but were off the highs with support coming from other bond markets especially bunds and Treasuries. The March bond future on LIFFE was trading at 128.53 up 0.24 from Tuesday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasuries trimmed some early gains, but remained higher. The early rise seen sponsored by foreign central bank buying. The March Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 112-18/32, up 01/32 from Tuesday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.65 percent.

JAPAN - The cash JGBs had a negative bias by late trading on Wednesday with the long-end hardest hit by portfolio reshuffling of institutional investors, traders said. In after hours trading the March future on LIFFE was trading at 125.53, down 0.34 from Tuesday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

EUROBONDS - The boundaries of eastern European debt markets were pushed back on Wednesday when the Croatian kuna became the newsest Eurocurrency. Croatia launched a 300 million kuna two-year Euro-domestic bond via Merrill Lynch and Zagrebacka Banka. The notes carry a 12.50 percent coupon and were priced at 98.50.

The Croatian finance ministry expected the bond's attractive terms would appeal to a broad range of retail and institutional investors. A syndicate manager at Merrill Lynch in London said he hoped final sales would be split 50-50 between domestic and international investors.
